strengths: Presents a practical, modular, training-free cascaded retrieval pipeline (sparse -> dense -> neural reranking) for table QA that avoids costly dataset-specific fine-tuning, which is a useful contribution for adaptability to new domains.

Provides reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each retrieval stage, query decomposition, table descriptions, and irrelevant-row filtering (Tables 5-10), which helps interpret where gains come from.
Includes an interesting robustness experiment under query paraphrasing, showing that CRAFT's cascade degrades far less than fine-tuned DTR variants, which is a meaningful practical finding.
Provides end-to-end QA evaluation across multiple LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Qwen2.5) and retrieval depths, plus a token-efficiency analysis (sub-table vs full-table) that is useful for practitioners.
Includes full prompts in the appendix, aiding partial reproducibility of the LLM-driven preprocessing steps.
weaknesses: The headline claim that CRAFT 'achieves better retrieval performance than SOTA sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers' is not well supported by the paper's own Table 1: THYME outperforms CRAFT substantially at R@1 (48.55 vs 41.13) and is competitive/better on average, undermining the central claim rather than merely nuancing it.

There appears to be a citation inconsistency/error: THYME is attributed to two different author sets (Da Li et al., 2025 and Weizhe Zhao et al., 2024) but cited with the same arXiv ID (2503.02251), and the introduction/methodology refer to 'the state-of-the-art framework (Zhao et al., 2024)' interchangeably with THYME (Li et al., 2025). This raises concerns about citation rigor and correctness.

The paper motivates the approach by contrasting with the 'high computational cost' of dense/fine-tuned retrieval, yet no latency, memory, or inference-cost comparison against baselines (including cost of the Gemini/OpenAI API calls used in preprocessing and reranking) is provided, leaving the core efficiency claim unsubstantiated.

Reliance on closed, versioned commercial APIs (Gemini-1.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Flash, text-embedding-3-small) for core pipeline steps undermines reproducibility and the 'training-free' framing, since these models can change or become unavailable, and no open alternative or sensitivity analysis is given.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (NQ-Tables), and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this, but no discussion or partial experiment on a second dataset (e.g., other open-domain TQA benchmarks) is attempted to support generalizability claims made in the abstract/conclusion.

No statistical significance testing or variance/repetition is reported for LLM-based end-to-end generation results, which can be stochastic, weakening confidence in reported F1 differences (e.g., few-shot vs zero-shot comparisons in Table 12 that are often within a point or two of each other).

Some comparisons (e.g., end-to-end results in Table 3 combining other retrievers' outputs with CRAFT's answer-generation pipeline, and Table 4 comparing against very different baseline systems RAG/DPR-RAGE/LI-RAGE with unclear matched conditions) are not clearly controlled, making it hard to isolate whether gains stem from retrieval quality, table representation (mini-tables), or prompt engineering.
The claim of 'outperforms all existing TQA-in-the-wild' in the introduction is vague, uncited, and not clearly substantiated by a specific comparison in the results.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant problem (scalable, adaptable table retrieval without dataset-specific fine-tuning) and proposes a sensible, modular cascade combining sparse retrieval, dense reranking, and LLM-based augmentation.

Extensive stage-wise ablations (Tables 8-12) isolate the contribution of each pipeline component (table descriptions, query decomposition, mini-table row filtering, neural reranking), giving useful insight into where gains come from.
The robustness experiment under query paraphrasing (Section 4.2) is a nice addition that DTR-based baselines lack, and shows CRAFT's cascade recovers most of the performance lost to rephrasing.
Efficiency analysis (token counts, embedding call counts) is detailed and provides a concrete quantitative case for the mini-table design.
Qualitative case studies (Appendix D) illustrating full-table hallucination vs mini-table correctness add useful diagnostic value beyond aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: The 'training-free'/'zero-shot' framing is undercut by the fact that dataset-specific model choices are made per benchmark (e.g., different embedding backbones for NQ-Tables vs OTT-QA, choice between text-embedding-3-small/large reported post hoc), and it is unclear whether these choices were selected using a held-out dev set or directly optimized against test-set recall, raising concerns about test-set leakage/overfitting in what is claimed to be a zero-shot method.

Comparisons framed as CRAFT 'outperforming SOTA' are not fully apples-to-apples: baselines are fine-tuned on the target dataset while CRAFT is not, yet CRAFT still benefits from per-dataset architecture/model tuning; the paper does not adequately caveat that this is not a fair zero-shot vs. supervised comparison in the same sense as typical zero-shot transfer evaluations.

On OTT-QA, CRAFT trails the best supervised hybrid baseline (THYME) by a nontrivial margin at R@1 (55.56 vs 66.67), and the end-to-end OTT-QA results are only reported in an oracle setting with gold passages, which is not a realistic open-domain evaluation and limits the paper's claims of 'strong zero-shot performance' on this benchmark.

The large-scale offline cost of using Gemini-1.5-Flash to generate titles/descriptions and sub-questions for every table (169K-419K tables) and every query is not discussed as part of the computational budget, despite efficiency being a central claimed contribution; this makes the 'training-free' cost savings arguably overstated relative to the true end-to-end resource footprint.

Reproducibility is undermined by the placeholder 'Code and data are available at:' with no actual link provided in the manuscript, and heavy reliance on proprietary, versioned APIs (Gemini, OpenAI embeddings) that can change over time, threatening long-term reproducibility.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided despite many close margins between CRAFT and competing methods (e.g., R@10/R@50 gaps of ~1 point on OTT-QA), making some 'competitive' claims hard to substantiate rigorously.

The contribution is largely an engineering integration of existing off-the-shelf components (SPLADE, sentence-transformers, OpenAI/Gemini embeddings, LLM-based augmentation) rather than a novel modeling or algorithmic advance, limiting the technical novelty relative to prior cascaded/hybrid retrieval work already cited (Re2G, THYME, DHR).

strengths: The paper conducts an extensive empirical evaluation, covering two benchmarks (NQ-Tables, OTT-QA), multiple retrieval stages, several downstream LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Qwen2.5, GPT-4o), and various values of retrieved-table depth n, which gives a fairly complete picture of the pipeline's behavior.

The robustness study using paraphrased queries (Table 4) is a useful addition that goes beyond standard recall metrics and shows the cascade is less brittle to query rephrasing than a single dense retriever.

The efficiency analysis (token counts, embedding call reduction, mini-table vs full-table context) is a concrete and practically relevant contribution, addressing real deployment costs of retrieval-augmented table QA.

The stage-wise ablations (Tables 9-12) clearly isolate the contribution of table descriptions, query decomposition, row filtering, and neural reranking, supporting the internal validity of the cascade design.
The qualitative case studies (Appendix D) illustrating why full-table context can hurt LLM answer extraction versus mini-table context are a nice complement to the quantitative results.
weaknesses: The claim of achieving 'SOTA' is overstated: on OTT-QA, CRAFT trails THYME by ~11 points and BIBERT+SPLADE by ~9 points at R@1 (Table 3), which is a substantial gap, yet the abstract and conclusion describe this as merely 'competitive' or nearly matching prior work; the framing does not adequately reflect the magnitude of this shortfall at the most stringent metric.

The comparison between CRAFT and fine-tuned baselines is confounded by encoder capability rather than isolating the effect of the cascaded, training-free design: CRAFT's best NQ-Tables numbers rely on text-embedding-3-large and Gemini-generated table descriptions/expansions, i.e., very large, recent, proprietary models, while baselines such as DTR, BIBERT, and THYME use much smaller, older encoders trained years earlier. It is unclear how much of the reported gain is attributable to the cascade architecture versus simply using stronger, more recent (and costly) pretrained backbones.

Similarly, the end-to-end comparison against LI-RAGE/DPR-RAGE (Table 6) pairs CRAFT with GPT-4o, a vastly more capable closed model than what the baselines used; this makes it difficult to attribute the F1 improvement to the retrieval pipeline itself rather than to the downstream reader model's capacity.

The OTT-QA end-to-end results are evaluated in an oracle setting where gold passages are supplied alongside retrieved tables, which is acknowledged as a limitation but substantially weakens the 'open-domain,' multi-hop claims emphasized in the abstract and title.

Reproducibility is a significant concern: the paper depends heavily on closed, commercial APIs (Gemini-1.5-Flash/2.5-Flash, text-embedding-3-small/large, gemini-embedding-001, GPT-4o) whose behavior, pricing, and availability can change over time, and the abstract's 'Code and data are available at:' link is left blank/unfilled, undermining the reproducibility that the paper explicitly promises.

No variance, multiple runs, or statistical significance testing is reported for any of the retrieval or end-to-end results, despite many close margins (e.g., R@10/R@50 differences of ~1 point against THYME), making it hard to assess whether reported gains are robust or within noise.

The methodological novelty is modest: cascaded sparse-to-dense retrieval with LLM-generated metadata augmentation is a fairly well-established pattern (as the related work section itself documents extensively), and the paper's contribution is primarily an engineering combination of existing off-the-shelf components rather than a new retrieval or representation technique.

Key pipeline hyperparameters (e.g., 5,000 candidates after Stage 1, 100 candidates after Stage 2, top-5 rows per mini-table) appear to be fixed heuristically without systematic justification or sensitivity analysis across datasets of very different scale (169K vs 419K tables).

strengths: Presents a modular, training-free cascaded retrieval pipeline (sparse → dense pruning → neural reranking) for open-domain table QA, evaluated on two established benchmarks (NQ-Tables, OTT-QA).

Comprehensive ablations isolating the contribution of each stage (Table 8-12) and of individual design choices such as table descriptions, query decomposition, and irrelevant-row filtering, which convincingly show that each pipeline component adds incremental recall.
Robustness experiment under query paraphrasing (Table 4) is a useful addition and shows CRAFT's cascade recovers performance better than a fine-tuned DTR baseline.
Practically useful efficiency analysis (embedding call counts, token-length reduction via mini-tables) that is relevant to real-world deployment concerns.

Informative qualitative error analysis/case studies illustrating why mini-table representations reduce hallucination compared with full-table context, even when the gold table is retrieved at a reasonable rank.
End-to-end QA results across multiple open- and closed-source LLMs (Llama3, Qwen2.5, Mistral, GPT-4o) provide a reasonably broad empirical picture of downstream utility.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading: the pipeline relies on an LLM (Gemini-1.5-Flash) to generate titles/descriptions offline for the entire corpus (169K and 419K tables). This is a substantial, dataset-specific preprocessing/adaptation cost that is not quantified (no reported latency or API cost for corpus-wide description generation), which undercuts the 'lightweight, plug-and-play' claim made in the abstract/contributions.

Overstated claims of state-of-the-art performance: on OTT-QA, CRAFT trails THYME and BIBERT+SPLADE at R@1 (55.56 vs. 66.67/64.72) and at R@10 (89.88 vs. 91.10/91.01), and on NQ-Tables CRAFT only leads at R@1 while being second-best at R@10 (underlined, not bolded) â€” yet the abstract/conclusion state CRAFT 'outperforms SOTA' and achieves 'new SOTA' without sufficiently qualifying these mixed results.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: CRAFT leverages large proprietary models (Gemini embeddings, OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, GPT-4o) that are far more expensive/capable than the baselines it is compared against (BIBERT, DTR, THYME use much smaller trained encoders), making the 'training-free vs. fine-tuned' narrative not a controlled comparison of comparable-capacity systems.

OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation uses an oracle setting with gold passages paired to retrieved tables, which is explicitly acknowledged as unrealistic but is still used to support claims of 'strong zero-shot performance' on OTT-QA in the abstract, creating a mismatch between the claim and the actual experimental setting.

Reproducibility is limited by heavy dependence on closed, versioned commercial APIs (Gemini Flash, GPT-4o, OpenAI embeddings, Gemini embeddings) whose behavior, availability, and pricing can change over time, and no cost/latency figures are given for the offline description-generation step that is central to the approach.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs; all numbers appear to be single-run point estimates despite stochastic components (LLM-generated descriptions, sub-question generation).

The core technical novelty is primarily in pipeline design/engineering (combining SPLADE, sentence embeddings, and commercial rerankers plus LLM-generated metadata) rather than in retrieval modeling itself, which somewhat limits the scientific contribution beyond a strong empirical recipe.

Minor clarity issues: some result descriptions in the text (e.g., 'new SOTA Recall@1') are not consistently reconciled with the tables where CRAFT is only marginally ahead or trails on other metrics/datasets, and the code repository link in the abstract is blank, raising a reproducibility concern if this is not solely due to anonymization.
